zh.title: 怎麼放下？佛陀教的七種斷除煩惱之法（一切漏經 MN2）
zh.seo_title: 怎麼放下執著與煩惱？佛陀在《一切漏經》教的七種具體方法
zh.seo_description: 想放下執著、放下煩惱，卻只找到「要放下」的空泛勸說？巴利《一切漏經》（MN 2）裡，佛陀不是只叫人放下，而是給出七種依情境選用的具體斷除法：由見、防護、受用、忍耐、迴避、驅除、修習。本頁逐段解說原文，並如實說明經文講的是「斷除諸漏（煩惱）」，其中最貼近「放不下的執念」的是驅除欲尋、瞋恚尋一法。
zh.question: 佛教怎麼「放下」執著和煩惱？有具體方法嗎？
zh.definition: 《一切漏經》（MN 2）是佛陀專講「怎麼斷除諸漏」的一部經。漏（āsava）指煩惱、影響並染污心的東西，其源頭包含欲漏、有漏、無明漏；它不完全等於中文口語的「執著」，但束縛人心、讓人放不下的欲念與瞋念正屬其中。面對這些漏，佛陀不是只說「放下」，而是給出七種依情境選用的做法——由見、由防護、由受用、由忍耐、由迴避、由驅除、由修習而斷。這是一套「有方法可照做」的框架，而非勵志口號。

sections.heading: 佛陀不是只叫你「放下」，而是給了七種方法
paragraphs: 很多人搜尋「怎麼放下」，得到的多半是「要放下」「別執著」這類話——聽起來對，卻不知道從哪裡下手。《一切漏經》難得的地方，就在於它把「放下」拆成了可操作的步驟。經文先點出總開關：不如理作意（把注意力放錯地方）時，未生起的煩惱會生起、已生起的會增長；如理作意時，未生的煩惱不生、已生的則被捨斷。也就是說，煩惱放不放得下，關鍵在於你怎麼看待、怎麼把注意力放到境上。
接著佛陀給出完整清單：有些漏應「由見」而斷，有些應「由防護」而斷，有些應「由受用、由忍耐、由迴避、由驅除、由修習」而斷（mn2:4.1）。七種方法對應七種情境——同樣是煩惱，來源不同，對治的手段也不同。這正是本經最實用之處：它不假設一招走天下，而是教你辨認眼前這個煩惱屬於哪一類，再選對應的做法。

sections.heading: 第一法・由見而斷：先看清「該想什麼、不該想什麼」
paragraphs: 七法之首是「由見而斷」，也就是用正確的見地釜底抽薪。經文很具體地指出：當一個人把注意力放在「不該作意的法」上，未生的欲漏會生起、已生的會增長，有漏與無明漏也是如此（mn2:6.2–6.4）。反過來，把注意力放對地方，這些漏就不生起、被捨斷。換句話說，很多執念不是靠硬壓，而是靠「看清楚它不值得一直想」而鬆開的。
那麼「看清」要看見什麼？經文說，如理作意「這是苦、這是苦的集起、這是苦的滅、這是導向苦滅的道跡」（四聖諦）的人，會捨斷三種結：有身見、疑、戒禁取（mn2:11.2–11.4）。這裡的「放下」，指的是放下錯誤的自我見與疑惑——放下的不只是某個念頭，而是撐起那些念頭的錯誤前提。

sections.heading: 防護與受用：從根門和日常用度下手
paragraphs: 第二法「由防護而斷」講的是守護根門。比丘審慮如理，以眼根律儀守護而住；經文說，對不守護眼根的人，惱熱的諸漏可能生起，對守護的人則不生起（mn2:12.2–12.3）。耳、鼻、舌、身、意也一樣。用現代話說：煩惱常常是從「多看一眼、多聽一句、任由念頭亂追」開始滾大的——在根門處收一收，很多執著根本不會成形。這是最前端、最省力的「放下」。
第三法「由受用而斷」則落在日常用度上。比丘如理省察後才受用飲食，不為享樂、不為驕逸、不為裝飾，只為維持此身、助益修行（mn2:14.1–14.2）。衣、住、藥也同樣以「夠用就好」的態度使用。這一法的智慧在於：對衣食住行擺正心態，就少了一整類因貪求受用而生的煩惱——放下，有時是先調整你和物質的關係。

sections.heading: 忍耐與迴避：對境不起煩惱的兩手
paragraphs: 第四法「由忍耐而斷」對治那些躲不掉的處境。比丘如理省察，成為能忍受者——忍受寒冷、炎熱、飢渴、蚊蟲之擾，以及粗魯不悅意的言辭、身上劇烈難耐的苦受（mn2:18.2）。經文說，對不忍受的人，惱熱的諸漏會生起，對忍受的人則不生起（mn2:18.3）。這裡的「放下」不是逃避，而是不對已經來到的不適再添一層瞋惱——境無法改變時，先放下對它的抗拒。
第五法「由迴避而斷」則是另一手：能避的就別硬碰。經文舉例，該避開的兇猛動物、蛇、坑穴、懸崖要避，不適當的座位、不適當的行境、以及惡友也要如理省察而完全迴避（mn2:19.3–19.4）。忍耐與迴避看似相反，其實互補：改變不了的境，用忍耐；能遠離的緣，就迴避。這對「放不下」的人是很實際的提醒——有些執著，是因為你一直把自己放在會勾起它的環境裡。

sections.heading: 第六法・由驅除而斷：最貼近「放下執念」的一法
paragraphs: 如果你要找的是「一個念頭卡在心裡放不下、該怎麼辦」，這一法最直接。「由驅除而斷」處理的正是已經在心裡升起的染污念頭。經文說，比丘如理省察，對已生起的欲尋（貪求的念頭）不忍受、捨棄、驅除、去除，使它達到滅盡；對已生起的瞋恚尋、惱害尋，以及凡生起的諸惡不善法，同樣不容留、捨棄、驅除、去除（mn2:20.2）。
值得注意的是用詞：對這些念頭是「不忍受」（nādhivāseti）——恰恰和第四法「忍耐」相反。這說明佛陀的方法是分情境的：對躲不掉的外境苦受用忍耐，對心裡冒出的貪念瞋念則不姑息、主動驅走。這裡的「放下」是主動的、當下的動作，而不是被動等它自己消失。經文說，不驅除的人會生起惱熱之漏，驅除的人則不會（mn2:20.3）——放不放得下，取決於你是否願意在念頭壯大前就把它請出去。

sections.heading: 第七法・由修習而斷：培養七覺支，趣向「完全放捨」
paragraphs: 前六法多半是「當下如何處理」，第七法「由修習而斷」則是長線工程：培養七覺支——念、擇法、精進、喜、輕安、定、捨。經文對每一覺支都用同一組修飾語：修習「依止遠離、依止離貪、依止滅、趣向完全放捨」的念覺支（mn2:21.2），乃至擇法、精進等（mn2:21.3–21.4）。
特別值得指出的是最後的捨覺支，同樣「趣向完全放捨」（vossaggapariṇāmiṁ，mn2:21.8）。這個「放捨」正是巴利經文裡最接近「放下」的方向：整套修習都朝向鬆手、離貪、止息。也就是說，最深的放下不是硬叫自己別在意，而是靠日積月累地培養這些覺支，讓心自然傾向於不抓取。前六法是止血，第七法是體質的改變。

sections.heading: 這對想「放下執著」的現代讀者意味什麼
paragraphs: 先說清楚一件事，才不會誤讀這部經：它的主角是「漏」（āsava，煩惱、染污心的東西），並不完全等同中文口語裡的「執著」。經文列的三種漏是欲漏、有漏、無明漏；其中最貼近日常說的「放不下的執念」的，是「由驅除而斷」那一法點名的欲尋、瞋恚尋（mn2:20.2）——貪求與怨怒的念頭。所以本頁用「放下煩惱／執著」承接你的搜尋，但如實地說：佛陀談的是斷除諸漏，範圍比「執著」更廣、更根本。

即便如此，這部經對想放下的人仍極有用，因為它把「放下」從口號變成了選單。經文開宗明義：是「知者、見者」才能讓諸漏滅盡，不是不知不見者（mn2:3.1）——放下需要看清，不是靠意志力硬撐。而全經的終點是：斷絕渴愛（taṇhā）、揭解結縛、徹底了知我慢而終結苦（mn2:22.2）。渴愛，才是佛教語境裡「執著」最核心的字。真正的放下，不是壓住某個念頭，而是連那個一直想抓住什麼的渴愛，都被看穿、鬆開。下次「放不下」時，不妨先問：這屬於七法裡的哪一類？是該看清、該防護、該忍、該避，還是該當場驅走？

zh.mahayana_note: 「放下」在後世佛教有豐富的開展。禪宗常說「放下著」「放下屠刀」，《金剛經》的「應無所住而生其心」更是漢傳語境裡「放下執著」的代表句，指心不黏著於任何對象而仍能起用；這與本經「趣向完全放捨」（vossagga）的方向相呼應，但表述脈絡不同。此外，大乘以「空」（śūnyatā）與「無所得」進一步把放下推及一切法，強調連「放下」之念亦不執取。這些是後世對放下的詮釋與發展；本頁僅呈現巴利《一切漏經》中「斷除諸漏」的具體教說，各系詮釋之間不做裁決。

faq.q: 佛教到底怎麼「放下」執著？有具體方法嗎？
faq.a: 有，而且不只一種。《一切漏經》（MN 2）記載佛陀給出七種依情境選用的斷除法：由見、防護、受用、忍耐、迴避、驅除、修習而斷。想放下卡在心裡的貪念、怨念，最直接的是第六法「由驅除而斷」——對已生起的欲尋、瞋恚尋不姑息，當場捨棄、驅走（mn2:20.2）。要根本改變，則靠第七法長期培養七覺支，讓心「趣向完全放捨」。
它是佛陀專門講「怎麼斷除諸漏（āsava，煩惱、染污心的東西）」的一部經，屬《中部》第二經。核心是七種斷除法的總綱與分述：不同來源的煩惱，要用不同的方法對治。全經最後以「斷絕渴愛、解開結縛、終結苦」作結（mn2:22.2）。

faq.q: 經文講的「漏」就是「執著」嗎？
faq.a: 不完全是。漏（āsava）指煩惱、影響並染污心的東西，經文列為欲漏、有漏、無明漏，範圍比中文口語的「執著」更廣。與「放不下的執念」最接近的，是驅除那一法點名的欲尋、瞋恚尋等貪瞋念頭（mn2:20.2）；而全經終點的「渴愛」（taṇhā，mn2:22.2）才是最貼近「執著」核心的字。本頁用「放下執著」承接讀者的問題，但依經文如實說明兩者不等同。

faq.q: 我一個念頭一直放不下，經文怎麼教？
faq.a: 對治「已經升起、揮之不去的念頭」，正是第六法「由驅除而斷」。經文教的是：對已生的欲尋、瞋恚尋、惱害尋不忍受、捨棄、驅除、去除，使它達到滅盡（mn2:20.2）。注意這裡刻意用「不忍受」，和對外境苦受用的「忍耐」相反——外境的苦要忍，心裡冒出的貪瞋念則要主動趕走，別讓它壯大。

faq.q: 為什麼光是勸自己「要放下」沒有用？
faq.a: 因為《一切漏經》一開頭就說，是「知者、見者」才能讓諸漏滅盡，不是不知不見者（mn2:3.1）。放下需要先看清這個煩惱屬於哪一類、值不值得一直想（由見而斷），再配合防護根門、忍耐、迴避、驅除、修習等具體手段。空喊「要放下」少了「看清」與「方法」這兩層，自然使不上力。

en.title: How Do You Let Go? The Buddha's Seven Methods for Removing Defilements (MN 2)
en.seo_title: How to Let Go of Attachment and Worry? The Buddha's Seven Concrete Methods in MN 2
en.seo_description: Tired of "just let it go" with no idea how? In the Pali Sabbāsava Sutta (MN 2) the Buddha gives not a slogan but seven situation-specific methods for removing the taints: by seeing, restraining, using, enduring, avoiding, dispelling, and developing. This page walks through the text and states honestly that it treats the removal of the āsavas (defilements), of which the closest to a "stuck thought" you can't drop is the dispelling of sensual and ill-willed thoughts.
en.question: How does Buddhism actually "let go" of attachment and worry—are there concrete methods?
en.definition: The Sabbāsava Sutta (MN 2) is the Buddha's dedicated discourse on how to remove the āsavas—the taints or defilements that flow into and stain the mind, whose sources include the taint of sensuality, of existence, and of ignorance. Āsava is not exactly the same as the colloquial "attachment," but the craving and aversion that keep a mind stuck are among them. Faced with these, the Buddha does not merely say "let go"; he gives seven methods to be chosen by situation—removal by seeing, by restraint, by using, by enduring, by avoiding, by dispelling, and by developing. It is a framework you can act on, not a motivational slogan.

sections.heading: The Buddha doesn't just say "let go"—he gives seven methods
paragraphs: Search "how do I let go" and you mostly get "you should let go" and "don't be attached"—true-sounding, but with no handle to grab. What makes the Sabbāsava Sutta unusual is that it breaks "letting go" into workable steps. It first names the master switch: with unwise attention (putting your attention in the wrong place), unarisen taints arise and arisen ones grow; with wise attention, unarisen taints do not arise and arisen ones are abandoned. Whether a defilement can be dropped hinges on how you regard it and where you place your attention.

The Buddha then gives the full checklist: some taints are to be abandoned by seeing, some by restraint, and others by using, by enduring, by avoiding, by dispelling, and by developing (mn2:4.1). Seven methods for seven situations—same category, defilement, but different sources call for different measures. This is the sutta's most practical feature: it assumes no single trick fits all, and teaches you to recognize which kind of defilement is in front of you, then pick the matching method.

sections.heading: Method 1 — by seeing: first get clear on what to attend to and what not to
paragraphs: First among the seven is removal "by seeing"—cutting the problem off at the root with right view. The text is concrete: when a person attends to "things not fit for attention," the unarisen taint of sensuality arises and the arisen grows, and so too the taints of existence and of ignorance (mn2:6.2–6.4). Conversely, attending to the right things means these taints do not arise and are abandoned. Many stuck thoughts loosen not by force but by seeing clearly that they are not worth dwelling on.

So what is one to see? The sutta says that a person who attends wisely to "this is suffering; this is its origin; this is its cessation; this is the path" (the four noble truths) abandons three fetters: identity view, doubt, and clinging to rules and observances (mn2:11.2–11.4). Here "letting go" means letting go of the mistaken view of self and of doubt—not merely a particular thought, but the false premises that prop such thoughts up.

sections.heading: Restraint and using: start at the sense doors and daily necessities
paragraphs: The second method, removal "by restraint," guards the sense doors. Reflecting wisely, a monk dwells restrained with the restraint of the eye faculty; the text says that for one who does not restrain the eye, distressing and feverish taints may arise, while for one who does, they do not (mn2:12.2–12.3). The same holds for ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. In modern terms: defilements often snowball from "one more look, one more word, letting the mind chase." Rein things in at the sense doors and many attachments never even form. This is the earliest, least costly form of letting go.

The third method, removal "by using," lands on daily necessities. A monk reflects wisely before using food—not for amusement, intoxication, or adornment, but only to maintain this body and support the practice (mn2:14.1–14.2). Robes, lodging, and medicine are used with the same "just enough" attitude. The wisdom here: set your attitude toward food, clothing, and shelter straight and you shed a whole class of defilements born of craving for consumption. Sometimes letting go begins by adjusting your relationship to material things.

sections.heading: Enduring and avoiding: two moves so situations don't stir defilement
paragraphs: The fourth method, removal "by enduring," meets the situations you can't dodge. Reflecting wisely, a monk becomes one who endures—cold, heat, hunger and thirst, the sting of insects, as well as rude and unwelcome speech and sharp, racking bodily pains (mn2:18.2). For one who does not endure, the text says, distressing and feverish taints may arise; for one who endures, they do not (mn2:18.3). "Letting go" here is not escape but refusing to add a layer of aversion onto discomfort that has already arrived—when the situation can't change, first let go of your resistance to it.

The fifth method, removal "by avoiding," is the complementary move: if you can steer clear, don't collide. The text gives examples—avoid the wild animal, the snake, the pit, the cliff; and, reflecting wisely, thoroughly avoid an unsuitable seat, an unsuitable resort, and bad friends (mn2:19.3–19.4). Enduring and avoiding look opposite but complement each other: endure what can't be changed; avoid the conditions you can distance yourself from. For anyone who "can't let go," this is a practical reminder—some attachments persist simply because you keep placing yourself where they get triggered.

sections.heading: Method 6 — by dispelling: the one closest to "dropping a stuck thought"
paragraphs: If what you're after is "a thought is stuck in my mind and I can't drop it—what do I do," this method is the most direct. Removal "by dispelling" deals precisely with the defiled thoughts that have already arisen in the mind. Reflecting wisely, the text says, a monk does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensuality (a craving thought)—he abandons it, dispels it, terminates it, brings it to non-existence; and likewise with an arisen thought of ill will, a thought of harming, and any evil, unwholesome states that arise (mn2:20.2).

Note the wording: toward these thoughts one "does not tolerate" (nādhivāseti)—the exact opposite of the fourth method's "enduring." This shows the Buddha's approach is situation-dependent: endure unavoidable external pain, but toward craving and hatred springing up in the mind, give no quarter—actively drive them out. This "letting go" is active and immediate, not passively waiting for a thought to fade. For one who does not dispel, distressing taints arise; for one who dispels, they do not (mn2:20.3)—whether you can let go depends on whether you're willing to show a thought the door before it grows.

sections.heading: Method 7 — by developing: cultivate the seven factors, inclining to "complete relinquishment"
paragraphs: The first six methods are mostly "how to handle it right now"; the seventh, removal "by developing," is the long game: cultivating the seven factors of awakening—mindfulness, investigation, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity. The text applies the same phrase to each factor: one develops the awakening factor of mindfulness "dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, ripening in relinquishment" (mn2:21.2), and likewise investigation, energy, and the rest (mn2:21.3–21.4).

Worth singling out is the last, the awakening factor of equanimity, likewise "ripening in relinquishment" (vossaggapariṇāmiṁ, mn2:21.8). This "relinquishment" (vossagga) is the term in the Pali text nearest to "letting go": the whole practice is oriented toward releasing, fading of desire, and cessation. The deepest letting go, then, is not forcing yourself not to care, but cultivating these factors day by day so the mind naturally inclines away from grasping. The first six methods stop the bleeding; the seventh changes the constitution.

sections.heading: What this means for a modern reader who wants to "let go of attachment"
paragraphs: One thing to be clear about, so the sutta isn't misread: its subject is the āsava (taint, that which defiles the mind), which is not exactly the colloquial "attachment." The three taints it lists are sensuality, existence, and ignorance; the nearest thing to the everyday "a stuck attachment" is the thought of sensuality and thought of ill will named in the method of dispelling (mn2:20.2)—thoughts of craving and resentment. So this page uses "letting go of attachment/defilement" to meet your search, while stating honestly that what the Buddha addresses is the removal of the taints, which is broader and more fundamental than "attachment."

Even so, the sutta is deeply useful for anyone wanting to let go, because it turns "letting go" from a slogan into a menu. It opens by declaring that it is "for one who knows and sees" that the taints are destroyed, not for one who neither knows nor sees (mn2:3.1)—letting go requires clear seeing, not sheer willpower. And the discourse ends at: having cut off craving (taṇhā), unraveled the fetter, and fully understood conceit, one has made an end of suffering (mn2:22.2). Craving is the word closest to the heart of "attachment" in the Buddhist context. True letting go is not pinning down a single thought, but seeing through and releasing even the craving that keeps reaching to grasp. Next time you "can't let go," ask first: which of the seven does this belong to—to be seen through, restrained, endured, avoided, or dispelled on the spot?

en.mahayana_note: "Letting go" was richly developed in later Buddhism. Chan/Zen speaks of "lay it down" and "put down the butcher's knife"; the Diamond Sutra's "one should give rise to a mind that does not abide anywhere" is the emblematic East Asian phrase for "letting go of attachment," meaning a mind that does not stick to any object yet still functions. This resonates with the present sutta's orientation toward "complete relinquishment" (vossagga), though the framing differs. The Mahāyāna further extends letting go to all phenomena through "emptiness" (śūnyatā) and "non-attainment," stressing that even the thought of "letting go" is not to be grasped. These are later interpretations and developments; this page presents only the concrete teaching on "removing the taints" found in the Pali Sabbāsava Sutta, and does not adjudicate among the traditions.

faq.q: How does Buddhism actually "let go" of attachment—are there concrete methods?
faq.a: Yes, and more than one. The Sabbāsava Sutta (MN 2) records the Buddha giving seven situation-specific methods for removal: by seeing, restraint, using, enduring, avoiding, dispelling, and developing. For a craving or resentful thought stuck in the mind, the most direct is the sixth—removal "by dispelling": don't tolerate an arisen thought of sensuality or ill will; abandon and drive it out on the spot (mn2:20.2). For lasting change, the seventh method cultivates the seven factors of awakening over time so the mind "inclines to complete relinquishment."

faq.q: What is the Sabbāsava Sutta about?
faq.a: It is the Buddha's dedicated discourse on how to remove the āsavas (taints—that which defiles and influences the mind), the second sutta of the Majjhima Nikāya. Its core is the outline and detailing of seven methods of removal: defilements of different sources call for different remedies. The discourse closes with "having cut off craving, unraveled the fetter, made an end of suffering" (mn2:22.2).

faq.q: Is the "taint" the text discusses the same as "attachment"?
faq.a: Not exactly. The āsava is a taint—that which flows into and defiles the mind—listed as the taints of sensuality, existence, and ignorance, broader than the colloquial "attachment." The closest to "a stuck attachment" is the thought of sensuality and thought of ill will named in the method of dispelling (mn2:20.2), while the "craving" (taṇhā) at the discourse's end (mn2:22.2) is nearest to the heart of "attachment." This page uses "letting go of attachment" to meet the reader's question, but states honestly, per the text, that the two are not identical.

faq.q: A thought keeps sticking and I can't let it go—what does the sutta teach?
faq.a: For an already-arisen, nagging thought, the relevant method is the sixth, removal "by dispelling." The text teaches: toward an arisen thought of sensuality, ill will, or harming, do not tolerate it—abandon, dispel, terminate, and bring it to non-existence (mn2:20.2). Note the deliberate "do not tolerate," the opposite of the "enduring" applied to external pain: endure outward hardship, but actively drive out craving and hatred springing up in the mind before they grow.

faq.q: Why doesn't simply telling myself to "let go" work?
faq.a: Because the Sabbāsava Sutta opens by saying it is "for one who knows and sees" that the taints are destroyed, not for one who neither knows nor sees (mn2:3.1). Letting go first requires seeing clearly which kind of defilement this is and whether it is worth dwelling on (removal by seeing), then combining that with concrete measures—guarding the sense doors, enduring, avoiding, dispelling, and developing. "Just let go" on its own lacks the two layers of clear seeing and method, so it can't get any traction.
